sections.text: Every asset is a .hasset file: a small chunked container whose chunks carry metadata, source data and cooked payloads (mesh vertex buffers, precompiled shaders, texture cook data, script language, graph JSON …). Assets are identified by UUID — references never break when files move. In the editor, a disk registry indexes loose assets by reading only their headers, so even huge projects resolve references without preloading. In a packaged game, assets live in the hpak archive and stream on demand, following the reference graph. Asynchronous loading runs on worker threads with main-thread registration under a frame budget.

sections.text: All of the engine's networking lives in one module, HorizonNet. It is a layered stack: sockets at the bottom, encryption over them, a message layer over that, and — at the top — two independent consumers that share everything below and nothing above. Layer What it does 0 — Transport ITransport and its implementations: TCP over IPv4 and IPv6, plus an in-process loopback used by the tests. 1 — Security SecureTransport, a decorator that adds a challenge-response handshake and encrypted frames to any transport. 2 — Session NetSession — message ids, a handler registry, connection bookkeeping — over BitStream, a bit-packed reader/writer with quantised floats. 3a — Gameplay GameReplication: server-authoritative snapshots for a running game. 3b — Collaboration CollabSession: several editors working on one project. Support NAT traversal, router diagnostics, the session directory client, and platform-native HTTP/HTTPS clients. Why the two top layers are separate Gameplay and collaboration share the transport and nothing above it, because their requirements are opposites. Collaboration replicates authored edits: rare, reliable, and they must never be lost — losing one silently discards somebody's work. Gameplay replicates simulation state: about thirty times a second, and loss-tolerant, because a dropped snapshot is corrected by the next one a few milliseconds later. Forcing gameplay down the collaboration path would make every position update a reliable, ordered message. Forcing collaboration down the gameplay path would quietly drop an edit. So they are two consumers, not one generalised system. What else uses the network The engine reaches the network in only a few other places, all through the same module's HTTP clients — which are platform-native (Apple, Windows and libcurl back-ends) rather than a bundled TLS stack: Feature Talks to Source control GitHub, GitLab and Azure DevOps APIs over HTTPS — see the editor manual. Session directory A small endpoint that maps a session id to a host address. Address discovery only. Router discovery SSDP multicast and SOAP on the local network, to ask for a port forward. There is no telemetry. The engine does not phone home, and nothing above is contacted unless you start a session, use source control, or ask for one explicitly.

The same discipline runs through the protocol. Lock subjects, presence selections, document scopes and the project key are all
to HorizonNet — it relays and compares them without ever interpreting them. What they mean is decided one layer up.

The session directory A host publishes where it can be reached under a short, high-entropy session id; a peer looks that id up. This is address discovery only — no session traffic ever passes through it. The division of responsibility is deliberate. The directory learns an address, a port and a display name. It never learns the join secret: authentication is engine-to-engine, so a compromised directory still cannot join or read a session. The server records the address it sees the request arrive from rather than one supplied in the body, so a client cannot point other peers somewhere else. Registering returns a management token, so merely knowing a session id is not enough to drop or hijack an entry. Anyone holding a session id learns the host's IP address. Ids are generated with high entropy and are short-lived for exactly that reason — treat one like a temporary invitation, not a name. Asking the router for a port Before publishing, the engine tries to open the way in by itself: it discovers the router with an SSDP multicast search, then asks for a port forward over UPnP, falling back to NAT-PMP. Routers generally speak one or the other — an Apple base station answers NAT-PMP and stays silent to SSDP entirely — so a UPnP failure says nothing about the second attempt. For IPv6, where there is no address translation to undo, it asks for a firewall pinhole instead. Then the directory tries to connect back. That verification matters: a mapping can succeed while the host is still unreachable, and publishing an endpoint nobody can dial produces a session that simply never works, with no clue why. When it cannot work A failed mapping is a normal outcome, not a bug. Many routers ship with UPnP disabled — it is a known attack surface — and corporate and campus networks block it deliberately. Behind carrier-grade NAT, common on mobile connections and some ISPs, there is no forwardable port at any level: not automatically, and not by hand either. The editor reports the router result and the reachability result separately, because they can disagree, and then says what you can actually do — forward the port yourself if the router is yours, otherwise put everyone on a mesh VPN such as Tailscale or ZeroTier, whose free tiers relay the traffic. Peers on the same local network always get through without any of it. Under CGNAT the advice deliberately omits manual forwarding: suggesting it would send someone off to spend an afternoon on something that cannot work. macOS Sequoia and later require the Local Network permission for the multicast discovery step. Without it the search fails while ordinary internet traffic keeps working — which looks like a routing bug rather than a missing permission. Grant it in System Settings » Privacy & Security » Local Network.

# host -> client, on success

SnapshotBegin
SnapshotChunk...     the scene, chunked (progress bar, bounded allocation)

# host -> everyone else
ParticipantJoined
# ...and on disconnect

The version check runs first, so a peer on an older build is told it has the wrong build rather than the wrong project — an older build does not send a project key at all, and reading a missing field would produce exactly that wrong answer. The snapshot is captured before the peer is admitted. If the host cannot produce one, the join is refused instead of completing with a peer that sits on an empty scene believing it is in sync. It is sent in chunks rather than as one blob so the joiner gets a progress bar and never has to accept an arbitrary allocation announced by the other side. Joining replaces the joiner's open scene — it does not merge into it. That is why the project check matters so much: before it existed, joining with the wrong project cost you your own scene and handed you one whose every asset reference dangled.

r.t: The per-item layer is what makes a shared graph feel live rather than reloaded. It is built on one generic message, and one idea.
One message for every document type

names a single item inside a single document: which asset, which document within it, what kind of item, which id, and either the item's JSON or a removal. HorizonNet interprets none of that. Because every graph and the element tree all decompose into identified items with a JSON form, one message type covers all eight editors — and a ninth costs no protocol work.
. Everything one edit produced travels as one frame, so pasting thirty nodes arrives atomically instead of interleaving with another peer's work.

A UI widget file holds both an element tree and a HorizonCode graph. They share a single lock — deleting an element breaks the nodes that reference it, so splitting the lock would only move the conflict from the lock table into the data — but they are addressed as separate
, so a delta can never land in the wrong one. Element ids and node ids are both small integers; the scope is what keeps them apart.
The editors are not instrumented to report what they changed. Each graph editor already reports only

something changed, and threading a per-action delta through every editor would have to be redone for every action added afterwards — the add menu, paste, box-select drags, every context menu, undo and redo.

Instead the engine keeps a shadow copy of each open document and diffs it. That covers every one of those paths at once, cannot drift from what the document actually holds, and only runs on the frames an editor reported a change. The shadow copy doubles as the echo guard: applying a peer's delta updates it in the same step, so their edit is never diffed back out as yours.
A single item's payload has a size bound. Past it the batch is

, and the whole-file path takes over for that change. Half a node's JSON is not a smaller edit — it is an unparseable one that would drop the item on the far side while looking like a success on yours.

r.t: The rules that hold across all of them
A change to the scene is a change you can take back.
Entities, terrain, placing a prefab — everything that touches the open world goes through the editor's own command path, so
takes it back in your history, in order, and in a collaboration session it is published to the others and refused when somebody else holds the lock.
A change to an asset file is not.

When a tool writes a material, an input mapping, a type definition or a particle emitter straight to disk, it is on disk the moment the answer comes back: the undo history is the scene's, not the content folder's, and there is no per-item publish for those in a session either — a lock held by a peer is checked and the call refused, but your co-workers learn of the edit when they reload. Git is the undo for that half.
Nothing changes while the game runs.
Every mutating tool is refused during play-in-editor, because an edit made then would be thrown away the moment you press stop and the world is restored.
An asset you are editing belongs to you.

If the asset a tool aims at sits in an open tab with unsaved changes, most families refuse the call rather than write the file behind your back — your next Save would have thrown the edit away. The HorizonCode and UI widget tools go the other way: they edit the document the tab is holding, take an undo snapshot the way your own edit would, and leave it to you to save. The widget tools say in their answer which of the two ways they went.
Listing changes nothing, including what is loaded.
The tools that list a folder answer from the file headers, so browsing never drags assets into memory. Asking about
material, widget or clip does load it — the answer cannot be assembled without it — and each of those tools says so in its own description.

The other kind of collaborator: a program on this machine, driving the editor the way a second person would. The editor carries a small MCP server — the protocol AI assistants speak to their tools — so a Claude session can place and move entities, set components, read the scene and author HorizonCode while you watch it happen in the viewport. It is off by default, and it never leaves this machine. Switching it on Preferences » Editor » Remote Control, one switch. The listener binds 127.0.0.1 only — never a network interface — and every connection has to present a token before it may say anything else. Listening Port at 0 lets the system pick one, which is the normal setting: the port is published together with the token in an endpoint file, and clients read it there rather than being told. That file is mcp-endpoint.json in your per-user data directory — ~/Library/Application Support/HorizonEngine on macOS, %APPDATA%\HorizonEngine on Windows, ~/.config/HorizonEngine on Linux. It holds the port, the token, the editor's process id and the host to dial. It is written with owner-only permissions when the listener comes up and deleted when it goes down, because an endpoint file that outlives its listener is a lie a client would act on. While the switch is on, anything running as you can read that file and change the scene. The token keeps another account on the same machine out; it does not keep your own programs out. That is why it is off by default, why it is per machine rather than per project, and why Restore Defaults switches it off even mid-session. MCP clients speak it over the standard input and output of a process they start themselves, and a GUI application cannot be that process — you started it, and it outlives any one client. So the editor ships he_mcp.py, a script that a client starts and that connects to whichever editor is currently listening. r.t: collects the things that happened without you doing them: a background scan that could not read a file, an import that finished, a collaboration request nobody answered, a peer that refused a file. It carries a count of what you have not read, and clicking it expands a flyout with the list.

It is not a log. A log answers “what happened”; this answers “what still needs you” — entries are written in sentences, and the ones about a particular file carry its path. Repeated identical messages collapse into one row with a count, and when the list is full it drops the oldest message you have already read, so an unread problem is never pushed out by a run of chatter.

sections.text: HorizonCode is Horizon Engine's visual scripting system — a Blueprint-style node graph you author in the editor, no text required. It is the same idea as the material editor, pointed at gameplay logic instead of shaders: you wire nodes together and the engine runs the graph. Every graph in the project — widget logic, level scripts, the GameInstance, standalone classes — runs on one central runtime, so graphs share state and events and can reference one another. r.t: Hybrid at runtime — nothing ever breaks
A graph that fails validation isn't a build error — it simply
, the reason is logged in the per-class report (

), and the rest of the export is unaffected. At runtime the game consults a compiled-class table first for every class it spawns; a hit runs native code, a miss (fallback, missing library, or an engine version mismatch) runs that one graph interpreted, exactly as the editor does. Compiled and interpreted instances live in the same runtime with the same ids, so references, event binding and cross-class calls work identically on both sides.
Behavioural parity is tested, not just intended: a contract suite runs a library of fixture graphs both interpreted and compiled and asserts

— same call order, same arguments, same results, same final variable state. Event cascades are bounded identically on both sides (dispatch recursion depth 32, 256 fires per cascade) so runaway Bind/Emit cycles can't hang either mode.
You don't have to export to find out whether a graph compiles — every graph editor has a
button that runs the same translation and either reports clean or highlights the offending node with a red halo.
requires a C++ toolchain on the exporting machine (the editor can install one — see
). It defaults on for Shipping profiles and off for Development, so day-to-day iteration never pays a build cost.

Note: Compile HorizonCode requires a C++ toolchain on the exporting machine (the editor can install one — see Preferences). It defaults on for Shipping profiles and off for Development, so day-to-day iteration never pays a build cost.

sections.text: How a script is attached and run, its lifecycle callbacks and the flat functions on horizon. Lua and Python share one underlying API, so the same calls are available in both — only the way you package a script differs. Every engine function, with its signature, is in the Engine API Reference. You attach a script to an entity with the Script component, which references a script asset by UUID plus a logical module name. Each script asset is either Lua or Python — the language is stored on the asset and is inferred from the file extension (.py -> Python, everything else -> Lua). Both languages are hosted side by side; an instance is routed to the right runtime automatically. Scripts run in the editor's Play Mode and in the exported game alike. When play mode starts, or when the game loads a scene, every entity that carries an enabled Script component gets one script instance bound to it; entities that arrive later, such as a streamed-in zone, get theirs when they load. Each instance is bound to its entity: the raw entity id is exposed as self.entityId in Lua and self.entity_id in Python. That id is the first argument to nearly every horizon function. Phase When Callback Start Once, when play mode begins (after property overrides are injected). onStart(self) / on_start(self) Update Every play-mode frame. dt is the elapsed time in seconds. onUpdate(self, dt) / on_update(self, dt) Collision enter When another physics body starts touching this entity. otherId is the other entity's id. onCollisionEnter(self, otherId) / on_collision_enter(self, otherId) Collision exit When another body stops touching this entity. onCollisionExit(self, otherId) / on_collision_exit(self, otherId) Every callback is optional — if a script doesn't define one, it's simply skipped. Collision callbacks only fire for entities that also have physics colliders. More callbacks: these four are the everyday ones. A script can also receive trigger overlaps, input actions, timers, animation notifies, UI clicks and hovers, multiplayer session events, replicated-variable changes, remote calls and anti-cheat reports. All of them, with their Lua and Python names, are listed under Callbacks in the Engine API Reference.

sections.text: The same functions are available in Lua (as the global horizon table) and Python (via import horizon). They come in two layers: the 35 flat functions below, which sit directly on horizon, and the groups horizon.math.*, horizon.physics.*, horizon.net.* and so on, generated from the engine's API registry. The groups are listed function by function in the Engine API Reference, together with the rules for passing vectors and entity ids. Entity arguments are the raw entity id. Invalid ids are tolerated: getters return neutral defaults, setters are no-ops. Arguments in brackets are optional. Function Returns Description log(message) — Writes a line to the Console panel and to HorizonEngine.log. The only way to reach the log row from a script: there is no horizon.log.* group. Reference getName(entity) string The entity's name, "" for an invalid id. Reference spawn(parent [, name]) entity Creates an empty entity named name (default "Entity") under parent and returns its id. parent 0 or invalid = top level. Unlike horizon.entity.spawn, the name is optional here. Reference destroy(entity) — Removes the entity; an invalid id is ignored. Check the id first: in a script 0 is the scene root, not “nothing”. Reference getPosition(entity) x, y, z Local position, i.e. relative to the parent. (0, 0, 0) for an invalid id. There is no horizon.transform.* group, so this is the only script route to the row. Reference setPosition(entity, x, y, z) — Sets the local position. On an entity with a rigid body or a character controller this is a teleport, so the physics step does not snap it back. Reference getRotation(entity) x, y, z Local Euler rotation in degrees. (0, 0, 0) for an invalid id. Reference setRotation(entity, x, y, z) — Sets the local Euler rotation in degrees; a teleport on physics bodies, like setPosition. Reference getScale(entity) x, y, z Local scale. (1, 1, 1) for an invalid id. Reference setScale(entity, x, y, z) — Sets the local scale. Reference raycast(ox, oy, oz, dx, dy, dz [, maxDist]) hit table / nil Casts a ray from the origin along the direction, up to maxDist (default 1000). Returns a flat table (Lua) / dict (Python) with the keys entity, x, y, z (hit point), nx, ny, nz (surface normal) and distance, or nil / None on a miss or without a physics world. horizon.physics.raycast answers the same question as ten return values and also reports the hit layer. Reference setVelocity(entity, vx, vy, vz) — Drives the character controller if the entity has one, its rigid body otherwise. No-op without a physics world. Reference isGrounded(entity) bool Whether the entity's character controller stands on ground. false without a physics world or a controller. Reference setMaterialParam(entity, name, x [, y, z, w]) bool Sets the node-graph material parameter name on the entity's material at runtime. One to four numbers, omitted ones are 0, so a scalar parameter takes just x. false when the entity has no material or the parameter does not exist. There is no horizon.material.* group. Reference getMaterialParam(entity, name) x, y, z, w Reads a material parameter back as four numbers; (0, 0, 0, 0) when it cannot be found. Reference setUIText(entity, text) — Replaces the text of the entity's UI Text component. Reference getUIText(entity) string The text of the UI Text component, "" without one. Reference setUIColor(entity, r, g, b [, a]) — Sets the element's primary colour: image tint, text colour or button normal colour, whichever exists (image first). a defaults to 1. Reference getUIColor(entity) r, g, b, a The primary colour in the same order; (1, 1, 1, 1) when there is none. Reference setUIVisible(entity, visible) — Switches the UI element on or off, together with everything under it. Reference isUIVisible(entity) bool Whether the UI element is switched on. Reference setUIPosition(entity, x, y) — Moves the element, in canvas units. Reference getUIPosition(entity) x, y The element's position in canvas units. Reference setUISize(entity, w, h) — Resizes the element, in canvas units. Reference getUISize(entity) w, h The element's size in canvas units. Reference setUIMaterialParam(entity, name, x [, y, z, w]) bool setMaterialParam for the material of the entity's UI Image. false without one or for an unknown parameter. Reference createWidget(assetPath) widget Instantiates the widget asset at the content-relative path and returns its id, 0 on failure. HorizonCode does the same with the Create Widget node. Reference destroyWidget(widget) — Removes the widget instance. Reference showWidget(widget) — Shows the widget on screen. Reference hideWidget(widget) — Hides it again; the instance and its state stay. Reference setWidgetZOrder(widget, z) — Draw order among widgets: higher is on top. Reference isWidgetVisible(widget) bool Whether the widget is currently shown. Reference callWidgetFunction(widget, name) bool Calls a public function of the widget's graph by name. false for a private or unknown function. Reference showCursor() — Releases the mouse and shows the pointer, e.g. for a menu. There is no horizon.cursor.* group. Reference hideCursor() — Hides the pointer and grabs the mouse again for camera control. Reference Time control: horizon.time.setTimeScale(s) dilates the game clock — 0 pauses, 1 is normal, up to 5. horizon.time.deltaTime() is already scaled, so a script that integrates against it slows down, speeds up and freezes without a single change; horizon.time.unscaledDeltaTime() hands the real frame time to anything that must keep running through a pause. Scripts, physics, cameras, animation and the day-night cycle all follow the scaled clock; the UI keeps the real one, so a pause menu can always unpause the game again. Physics functions (raycast, setVelocity, isGrounded) need an active physics world. Without one, raycast returns a miss, isGrounded returns false and setVelocity is a no-op. The raycast hit table A hit is a flat table (Lua) / dict (Python) — the point and normal are spread across individual keys, not nested: Key Meaning entity Id of the entity that was hit. x, y, z The hit point in world space. nx, ny, nz The surface normal at the hit point. distance Distance from the ray origin to the hit.

r.t: And a working example in each language — a mover that logs its name, spawns a child, and drives its own transform every frame:

blocks.text:
local M = {}

M.properties = { speed = 2.0 }

function M.onStart(self)
    self.t = 0
    horizon.log("Patroller start: " .. horizon.getName(self.entityId))
    -- spawn a marker parented to this entity
    self.marker = horizon.spawn(self.entityId, "Marker")
end

function M.onUpdate(self, dt)
    self.t = self.t + dt
    local x = math.sin(self.t) * self.speed
    horizon.setPosition(self.entityId, x, 0, 0)
end

function M.onCollisionEnter(self, otherId)
    horizon.log("Hit " .. horizon.getName(otherId))
end

return M
blocks.title: patroller.lua

blocks.text:
import horizon
import math

class Patroller(horizon.Behavior):
    speed = 2.0

    def on_start(self):
        self.t = 0.0
        horizon.log("Patroller start: " + horizon.getName(self.entity_id))
        # spawn a marker parented to this entity
        self.marker = horizon.spawn(self.entity_id, "Marker")

    def on_update(self, dt):
        self.t += dt
        x = math.sin(self.t) * self.speed
        horizon.setPosition(self.entity_id, x, 0, 0)

    def on_collision_enter(self, other_id):
        horizon.log("Hit " + horizon.getName(other_id))

sections.text:
Every function on this page comes from one table inside the engine, the API registry. A HorizonCode graph, a Lua script, a Python script and C++ game code all call the same row, so a function behaves the same in all four. What differs is how you spell the call and how arguments travel. These rules apply to every row below. One function, four names Frontend How physics.addImpulse is called HorizonCode the node Add Impulse (search the node menu by that name) Lua horizon.physics.addImpulse(self.entityId, 0, 5, 0) Python horizon.physics.addImpulse(self.entity_id, 0, 5, 0) C++ inside the engine HE::api::physics::addImpulse(ctx, entity, {0, 5, 0}) C++ game module he::physics::addImpulse(entity, {0, 5, 0}), where a service helper exists The C++ name listed with every row is the engine's own function behind it. A native GameLogic module does not link against the engine and cannot call it; it reaches a smaller set (save, entity lookup, physics, input, content, networking and anti-cheat) through the he:: service helpers, see Native C++. Function names are camelCase in Python too: horizon.physics.addImpulse, not add_impulse. Four groups are not reachable as horizon.<group>.* from Lua and Python: transform, material, cursor and log. Scripts use the flat functions for them instead (horizon.setPosition, horizon.setMaterialParam, horizon.showCursor, horizon.log). Rows without a flat twin, such as transform.getWorldPosition, are HorizonCode and C++ only. Each group below says which case it is. Arguments and results Arguments are passed flat, in the order the signature lists them. A vector is spread into its numbers, it is not a table or a tuple: Type in the signature Lua Python float one number one float (an int is accepted) int, entity, ref, enum one integer one int bool true / false True / False string one string one str vec2 2 numbers: x, y 2 numbers vec3 3 numbers: x, y, z 3 numbers color, vec4 4 numbers: r, g, b, a 4 numbers struct one table with __type one dict with "__type" Results spread the same way. One value comes back as that value, several as Lua multiple return values or a Python tuple, none as nil / None. physics.raycast takes two vec3 and a float (seven numbers) and returns a bool, an entity, two vec3, a float and an int (ten values): ground.lua local x, y, z = horizon.getPosition(self.entityId)
local hit, other, px, py, pz, nx, ny, nz, dist, layer =
    horizon.physics.raycast(x, y, z,  0, -1, 0,  50)
if hit then
    horizon.log("ground is " .. dist .. " below")
end ground.py x, y, z = horizon.getPosition(self.entity_id)
hit, other, px, py, pz, nx, ny, nz, dist, layer = \
    horizon.physics.raycast(x, y, z,  0, -1, 0,  50)
if hit:
    horizon.log(f"ground is {dist} below") Too few arguments is an error: Lua raises bad argument #n … (number expected, got no value), Python raises IndexError. The one exception is a missing bool in Lua, which silently reads as false. Extra arguments are ignored in both languages. Optional arguments exist only where a signature shows them in brackets, which is only on the flat functions. Entity ids and “Self” An entity is passed as its integer id: self.entityId in Lua, self.entity_id in Python, or whatever a lookup like horizon.entity.findByName returned. Invalid ids are tolerated: getters return a neutral default, setters do nothing. Always pass your own id. Parameters marked self in HorizonCode mean “the calling object” when a graph leaves the pin unconnected. A Lua or Python script is not such an object, so there it does not apply: 0 is passed on unchanged, the engine logs “Entity is empty and there is no calling object”, and the call acts on entity 0, the scene root. Write horizon.entity.getName(self.entityId), never horizon.entity.getName(0). List results (not yet usable from scripts) A few rows return a list, such as physics.overlapSphere, physics.raycastAll, fs.list, save.list or scene.available, and process.run takes one. HorizonCode and C++ handle these fine. The Lua and Python bridge does not yet translate lists: such a call currently returns a single 0 or "" instead of the list. These rows are marked list: HorizonCode/C++ only below. Until the bridge is fixed, use them from a HorizonCode graph. Events in the descriptions The descriptions come from the editor and name HorizonCode events such as On Timer or On Http Response. A script receives only the events listed under Callbacks; those are linked where they appear. The others (On Http Response, On File Changed, On Menu Item, On Tray Item, On Row Bind, On Window Closed, On Dismissed, On Selection Changed, On Right Clicked) have no Lua or Python callback today. Where a query exists, poll it instead, for example horizon.http.done(ticket) each frame after horizon.http.get. Otherwise handle that part in a HorizonCode graph. Actions and queries Every row is either an action (it changes something: moves, spawns, plays, writes) or a query (it only reads and returns). In HorizonCode an action is a node with white execution pins that runs in sequence, a query is a data node without them. In a script both are ordinary calls, but the tag tells you whether a call is safe to repeat freely. Project permissions A few rows reach outside the game and only run when the project allows it, under Project Settings » Permissions. Without the permission the call does nothing and returns its “failed” value (false, 0, an empty result), and the log says which permission is missing. The settings travel into the exported app, and they bind play mode in the editor the same way. Permission Rows Files outside the project fs.* with an absolute path that the user did not pick in a file dialog, print.toPdf, db.open Run other programs process.run, process.openUrl, print.file, app.setAutostart Network access http.get, http.post Dialogs and the clipboard need no permission. Remote calls take any arguments horizon.net.callServer(entity, name, …), horizon.net.callClient(player, entity, name, …) and horizon.net.callAllClients(entity, name, …) accept any number of extra arguments after the function name and pass them on. Their types are taken from the values themselves: a boolean, an integer, any other number, a string, or a list/table of those. This is the one place where the registry signature (which has no slot for them) does not describe the script call. The receiving side is a method of that name on the target entity's script, see Callbacks.

What Lua Python Enum entry (an integer) horizon.enums.Weapon.Sword horizon.enums.Weapon.Sword New struct with its default values horizon.structs.Loadout() -> table horizon.structs.Loadout() -> dict A struct value is a plain table / dict: one key per field plus __type, the path of the struct asset. Keep __type when you hand the value back, it is how the engine knows which struct it is. Missing fields keep their defaults, unknown keys are ignored. Inside a struct, fields are single values rather than spread: a vec2 is {x, y} / [x, y], a colour {r, g, b, a}, a transform {pos = {…}, rot = {…}, scl = {…}}, a list a sequence, and a nested struct a nested table. A map field is a Python dict (it keeps its order); in Lua it is a table plus a __keys list that holds the order. Structs go in and out of save.setStruct / save.getStruct this way.

sections.text:
A Lua script returns a table of functions, a Python script defines one subclass of horizon.Behavior. The engine calls the functions below on it by name; every one is optional, and a missing one is simply skipped. Lua names are camelCase, Python names snake_case. Receives says who gets the call: this entity means only the script on the entity concerned, every script means every Lua and Python instance in the session, so check the arguments before reacting. Results of many calls on this page arrive here: timers, input actions, network events, anti-cheat reports. Lifecycle Lua / Python Receives When onStart(self)
on_start(self) this entity Once, when the script starts: at the start of play mode, in a packaged game when its scene loads, and for scripts on entities that arrive later (an additive zone). Exposed properties are already set. onUpdate(self, dt)
on_update(self, dt) this entity Every frame. dt is the scaled frame time in seconds (0 while the game is paused through horizon.time.setTimeScale(0)). Physics contacts Both entities of a contact get the event, each with the other's id. A contact where either side no longer exists is dropped entirely. A trigger contact fires both pairs: onCollisionEnter and onBeginOverlap, then onCollisionExit and onEndOverlap. Lua / Python Receives When onCollisionEnter(self, other)
on_collision_enter(self, other) this entity Another physics body starts touching this entity. onCollisionExit(self, other)
on_collision_exit(self, other) this entity It stops touching. onBeginOverlap(self, other)
on_begin_overlap(self, other) this entity Something enters a trigger collider on this entity, or this entity enters one. onEndOverlap(self, other)
on_end_overlap(self, other) this entity The overlap ends. Input actions Actions are the ones defined in the project's input mapping. These go to every script instance, not only to the player's entity; pick the action by name. For polling instead of events use horizon.input.actionDown and friends. Lua / Python Receives When onInputPressed(self, name)
on_input_pressed(self, name) every script A button action went down this frame. onInputReleased(self, name)
on_input_released(self, name) every script A button action went up this frame. onInputAxis(self, name, value)
on_input_axis(self, name, value) every script Every frame, for each 1D axis action, with its current value (not multiplied by dt). onInputAxis2D(self, name, x, y)
on_input_axis2d(self, name, x, y) every script Every frame, for each 2D axis action. Note the lower-case d in the Python name. Timers Lua / Python Receives When onTimer(self, handle)
on_timer(self, handle) every script A timer started with horizon.timer.after or horizon.timer.every went off. handle is the value those calls returned; compare it to tell your timers apart, because every instance receives every timer. Timers run on real time, a paused game does not stretch them. Animation notifies Lua / Python Receives When onAnimationNotify(self, name)
on_animation_notify(self, name) this entity The entity's animation passed a single-frame notify called name. onAnimationNotifyBegin(self, name)
on_animation_notify_begin(self, name) this entity A notify state (a notify with a duration) started. onAnimationNotifyEnd(self, name)
on_animation_notify_end(self, name) this entity The notify state ended. In-game UI pointer Sent to scripts on entities with an interactive UI element (a button, or any element carrying a script) under the mouse. Lua / Python Receives When onClick(self)
on_click(self) this entity The element was clicked: pressed and released over it. onHoverEnter(self)
on_hover_enter(self) this entity The pointer moved onto the element. onHoverExit(self)
on_hover_exit(self) this entity The pointer left it. Multiplayer session Every script instance receives these, on host and client alike. Lua / Python Receives When onConnected(self)
on_connected(self) every script This client finished connecting to a host. onDisconnected(self, reason)
on_disconnected(self, reason) every script The connection ended; reason is the numeric reason code. onPlayerJoined(self, player)
on_player_joined(self, player) every script A player joined; player is their connection number. onPlayerLeft(self, player)
on_player_left(self, player) every script A player left. onSessionStarted(self)
on_session_started(self) every script A session started (hosting or joined). onSessionEnded(self)
on_session_ended(self) every script The session ended. Replication and remote calls Lua / Python Receives When onRep_<var>(self, old)
on_rep_<var>(self, old) this entity A replicated variable (declared with horizon.net.declareVarInt and its siblings) arrived with a new value on this client. Never called on the host, which set the value itself. <var> is the variable's name verbatim (health gives onRep_health / on_rep_health); old is the previous value. Read the new one with horizon.net.getVarInt and its siblings. <name>(self, …)
<name>(self, …) this entity A remote call from horizon.net.callServer, callClient or callAllClients runs the method of exactly that name on the target entity's script, with the caller's extra arguments. No renaming between languages: a Lua takeDamage is reached by a Python caller as takeDamage. Anti-cheat Lua / Python Receives When onCheatDetected(self, reportId)
on_cheat_detected(self, reportId) every script The host's anti-cheat filed a report. Read it with horizon.anticheat.reportLevel, reportRule, reportPlayer … and override the host's reaction with horizon.anticheat.respond in the same frame.

vars.text:
local M = {}

-- True when target lies within coneDeg degrees around the direction
-- (fx, fy, fz) this entity faces.
function M.canSee(self, target, fx, fy, fz, coneDeg)
    local x, y, z = horizon.getPosition(self.entityId)
    local tx, ty, tz = horizon.getPosition(target)
    local dx, dy, dz = horizon.math.normalize3(tx - x, ty - y, tz - z)
    local limit = horizon.math.cos(horizon.math.radians(coneDeg / 2))
    return horizon.math.dot3(dx, dy, dz, fx, fy, fz) >= limit
end

return M

Lua / Python: horizon.math.<function> · C++: HE::api::math::<function> Pure functions over numbers: none of them changes anything, so they can be called anywhere and as often as needed. In a script the language's own math library does most of this too, and with more precision. horizon.math is for the results a HorizonCode graph would get, and for what the languages lack: lerp, clamp, the vector helpers and 32-bit bit operations. Angles. sin, cos, tan and atan2 work in radians, while the engine's rotations are in degrees. radians and degrees convert between them; horizon.math.sin(90) is 0.894, not 1. Precision. Every float crosses into the engine as a 32-bit number, about seven significant digits: normalize3(3, 0, 4) returns 0.6000000238…, 0, 0.8000000119…. Compare results with a tolerance, not with ==. Vectors are spread like every other argument: length(x, y), distance3(ax, ay, az, bx, by, bz). normalize3 and cross return three numbers. Bit operations (bitAnd to shiftRight) take and return 32-bit signed integers. Lua accepts an integer or a float with no fraction (6.0); 6.5 raises number has no integer representation. Python accepts only an int; any float raises TypeError. Results wrap at 32 bits: shiftLeft(1, 31) is −2147483648. Example: math.dot3 view_cone.lua local M = {}

Lua / Python: horizon.string.<function> · C++: HE::api::str::<function> Text functions with the same results a HorizonCode graph gets. Three rules decide most surprises: Positions count from 0, also in Lua, whose own string.sub and string.find count from 1. find returns −1 when the piece is not there. Lengths and positions are bytes. Text is UTF-8: letters, digits and punctuation from plain ASCII take one byte, an accented or non-Latin letter two to four. length("ä") is 2, and a substring can cut such a letter in half. toUpper and toLower change only A to Z. Comparisons are exact. equals, contains, find, startsWith and endsWith are case-sensitive; lower both sides first when case should not matter. An empty piece is found everywhere: contains(s, "") is true and find(s, "") is 0, while replace(s, "", x) returns s unchanged. A negative start in substring uses up part of count, so substring("hello", -2, 4) is "he". toNumber reads the number at the start of the text and ignores the rest: "3.5abc" gives 3.5, " 42 " 42, "1e3" 1000 and "0x10" 16. local M = {}

function M.onStart(self)
    -- Without this, every launch rolls the same numbers. Seed in one

function M.onInputPressed(self, name)

    if horizon.time.isPaused() then
        horizon.time.resume()

Lua / Python: horizon.time.<function> · C++: HE::api::time::<function> The game clock. It advances once per frame, and every query gives the same answer for the rest of that frame. In the editor it runs only during Play and starts from 0 each time. For the time of day use Date and Time; to be called back later, use a Timer. deltaTime and elapsed are scaled: they follow the time scale and stand still while the game is paused or in a hit stop. unscaledDeltaTime and unscaledElapsed follow real time, which is what a pause menu or a UI animation needs. Three separate controls stop or slow the clock, and effectiveScale is their result: Time scale (setTimeScale), limited to 0…5. A larger value becomes 5, a negative one 0. Pause (pause / resume). It also silences input actions, except the ones with Fires while the game is paused ticked in the Input asset. Tick it on the key that opens the pause menu, or that key cannot close it again. All scripts and graphs share one pause, so a resume anywhere lifts a pause from anywhere. The pause the window sets when it loses focus is separate; resume cannot lift it. Hit stop (hitStop): a freeze for a stretch of real time. Input keeps arriving, and isPaused stays false. Pause and hit stop leave the time scale alone, so the game resumes at the speed it had. When a game loads another scene, the scale goes back to 1 and the script pause and any hit stop are lifted; elapsed and frameCount keep counting. Example: time.pause pause_menu.lua local M = {}

Lua / Python: horizon.json.<function> · C++: HE::api::json::<function> Reading and writing JSON text without a parser of your own: a config file from File System, a reply from HTTP. Every call takes the whole document as a string. The setters do not change it in place; they return the new document, so keep the result: doc = horizon.json.setNumber(doc, "volume", 0.8). A path is a chain of keys separated by dots, with [i] for an array element counted from 0: user.name, items[2].id. The empty path is the document itself, so count(text, "") counts a top-level array. A key that itself contains a dot cannot be reached. Getters never fail loudly. A missing path, a value of another type and text that is not JSON all return the fallback. has is true for a key whose value is null. Setters create missing objects along the path, and an empty string starts a new document. They cannot add array elements: a path through a missing index, or through a value that is not an object, returns the document unchanged, as does text that is not JSON. The returned text is compact and its keys come out in alphabetical order, whatever order they had. Numbers pass through a 32-bit float. getNumber is exact for whole numbers up to 16 777 216 and keeps about seven digits otherwise; setNumber writes 3 as 3.0 and 0.1 as 0.10000000149011612. Lua / Python: horizon.debug.<function> · C++: HE::api::debug::<function> Lines, spheres and boxes drawn into the 3D view, to see what a script is doing: where a ray went, what an overlap covered. A shape stays for seconds; 0 draws it for one frame, so a shape that follows something moving is drawn again every frame from onUpdate. seconds counts down in real time, so a paused game does not keep a shape alive longer; in the editor the countdown runs only during Play. The color is red, green and blue from 0 to 1; its alpha is ignored. clear removes every shape, including the ones other scripts drew. Debug shapes appear in a packaged game too, so take them out, or put them behind a flag of your own, before you ship. Known issue: four numbers per position. The positions of line, sphere and box are declared as colors, so Lua and Python read four numbers for each one. Pass a fourth number (it is ignored) after every x, y, z: line takes 13 arguments, not 10. With too few, Lua reports bad argument #11 and Python raises IndexError. The signatures below show the extra number as _. Example: debug.line ground_probe.lua local M = {}

function M.onUpdate(self, dt)
    local x, y, z = horizon.getPosition(self.entityId)
    -- Four numbers per position and color, the fourth is ignored.
    -- 0 seconds: drawn this frame only, so the shapes follow the entity.
    horizon.debug.line(x, y, z, 0,   x, y - 2, z, 0,   1, 0, 0, 1,   0)
    horizon.debug.sphere(x, y - 2, z, 0,   0.25,   0, 1, 0, 1,   0)
end

return M ground_probe.py import horizon

class GroundProbe(horizon.Behavior):
    def on_update(self, dt):
        x, y, z = horizon.getPosition(self.entity_id)
        # Four numbers per position and color, the fourth is ignored.
        # 0 seconds: drawn this frame only, so the shapes follow the entity.
        horizon.debug.line(x, y, z, 0,   x, y - 2, z, 0,   1, 0, 0, 1,   0)
        horizon.debug.sphere(x, y - 2, z, 0,   0.25,   0, 1, 0, 1,   0) Function Returns Description line(x1, y1, z1, _, x2, y2, z2, _, r, g, b, _, seconds) — Draws a line in the world for Seconds (0 = this frame only). A packaged game draws it too, so take debug drawing out before you ship.

Lua / Python: horizon.entity.<function> · C++: HE::api::entity::<function> Creating, finding and removing entities. An entity is an integer id (see Entity ids). When a destroyed entity's slot is reused, the newcomer gets a different, larger id, so a kept id never points at a stranger; it just stops existing. Guard it with exists. exists(0) is false: 0 is what findByName returns when it finds nothing, even though it is also the scene root. destroy takes the entity's children with it. spawnClass and spawnClassRotated need the running game or play mode; they return 0 and log the reason when the class path is unknown or not an Entity class. The path is the class asset's content path, as in the Content Browser. self, selfObject and the Ref rows (instance, owned, destroyObject) belong to HorizonCode objects. A Lua or Python script is not one, so self() and selfObject() always return 0 there; use self.entityId / self.entity_id. Visibility only affects drawing. An entity with nothing to draw always reports getVisible = true, also right after setVisible(e, false). Known issue: spawn creates no transform. The new entity has a name and a parent, but no Transform component, so setPosition, setRotation and setScale on it do nothing and getPosition returns 0, 0, 0 (measured on build 7d49d44f, also for the flat horizon.spawn). Until this is fixed, spawn a class with spawnClass, or give an entity its position by placing it in the scene. saveState, hasSavedState and applySavedState store an entity's pose and visibility in the active save, keyed by the entity's stable UUID, so the same entity finds its state again after the scene is loaded anew. Three things must hold, and each missing one logs its own warning and returns false: the game is running (play mode or the packaged game), a save is active (save.create / save.load), and the entity has an enabled Save State component, whose checkboxes choose what is stored. Nothing is on disk until save.write. Example: entity.exists boss_gate.lua local M = {}

-- loads hidden, 200 m along X, while the player walks; the door shows it.

end

-- "Interact" is an input action.
function M.onInputPressed(self, name)

Lua / Python: horizon.scene.<function> · C++: HE::api::scene::<function> Every call that changes scenes is a request: it is queued and carried out at the start of the next frame, before any script's onUpdate, in the order it was made. So the code after load still runs in the old scene, and a zone you just loaded is not there yet: zonePosition returns 0, 0, 0 and zoneScene an empty string until the next frame. Show, hide and move requests made right after loadAdditive still apply to the new zone, because they queue behind it. Scene paths are relative to the project folder, for example Scenes/Level2.hescene. Switching (load) replaces the whole scene. With hidden = true it only preloads the scene and its assets; hasPendingLevel turns true, and activate swaps it in without a loading hitch. A second hidden load replaces the pending one. Zones (loadAdditive) add a scene next to the current one, at a world offset, and return a zone id at once. Zone ids count up from 1 and are never reused. A hidden zone is loaded and simulated but not drawn until showZone. A zone gets collision, and in the packaged game its scripts start when it arrives. In the editor's play mode zones work, but load and activate only log “runs in the packaged game” and keep the current scene. Leaving play mode removes every zone again. Example: scene.loadAdditive cave_stream.lua local M = {}

A save follows a SaveGame Template asset, which lists its fields and their defaults; the project's default template (Project Settings) is the one create uses. One save is active at a time and every field call works on it, in memory, until write puts it on disk as Saves/<id>.json in the game's data folder (see File System). write replaces the file in one step, so a crash leaves the old save or the new one, never half of each. vars.text:
local M = {}
local REACH = 2.0   -- metres in front of the character
local PUSH  = 4.0   -- impulse, newton-seconds

-- "Interact" is a button action. Pushes whatever dynamic body is in front.
function M.onInputPressed(self, name)
    if name ~= "Interact" then return end
    local e = self.entityId
    local x, y, z = horizon.getPosition(e)
    local _, yaw = horizon.getRotation(e)
    local r = horizon.math.radians(yaw)
    local fx, fz = -horizon.math.sin(r), -horizon.math.cos(r)   -- facing, -Z at yaw 0
    -- Start a step ahead: a ray from inside the own capsule would hit it.
    local ox, oz = x + fx * 0.75, z + fz * 0.75
    local hit, other, px, py, pz = horizon.physics.raycast(ox, y, oz, fx, 0, fz, REACH)
    if hit and horizon.physics.hasPhysics(other) then
        -- The hit point is world space, which is what AtPosition expects.
        horizon.physics.addImpulseAtPosition(other, fx * PUSH, 0, fz * PUSH, px, py, pz)
    end
end

return M

import horizon

class PushCrate(horizon.Behavior):

        ox, oz = x + fx * 0.75, z + fz * 0.75
        hit, other, px, py, pz, *_ = horizon.physics.raycast(ox, y, oz, fx, 0, fz, REACH)
        if hit and horizon.physics.hasPhysics(other):
            # The hit point is world space, which is what AtPosition expects.
            horizon.physics.addImpulseAtPosition(other, fx * PUSH, 0, fz * PUSH, px, py, pz)

local M = {}
local FLOOR = -20   -- below this height the character has fallen out

function M.onStart(self)
    self.sx, self.sy, self.sz = horizon.getPosition(self.entityId)
end

function M.onUpdate(self, dt)
    local _, y = horizon.getPosition(self.entityId)
    if y < FLOOR then
        -- Back to where the level started it, without the speed of the fall.
        horizon.physics.setPositionAndReset(self.entityId, self.sx, self.sy, self.sz)
    end
end

return M

local M = {}

-- On an entity with a Nav Agent. World positions on the baked NavMesh.
local POINTS = { {6, 0, -6}, {6, 0, 6}, {-6, 0, 6} }

local function goNext(self)
    self.i = self.i % #POINTS + 1
    local p = POINTS[self.i]
    if not horizon.nav.moveTo(self.entityId, p[1], p[2], p[3]) then
        horizon.log("patrol point " .. self.i .. " is not reachable")
    end
end

function M.onStart(self)
    self.i = 0
    goNext(self)
end

function M.onUpdate(self, dt)
    -- isMoving turns false on arrival (and after a refusal).
    if not horizon.nav.isMoving(self.entityId) then goNext(self) end
end

return M

rows.t: moveTo(entity: int, x: float, y: float, z: float)

Sends a Nav Agent walking to a world position: the route across the baked nav mesh is searched right here, and then followed over the next frames without anything else being called. The one node an enemy needs in order to come after the player. It answers whether the walk started, and the answer is worth branching on, because a false means the agent will not move at all: no nav mesh has been baked, the destination is off the walkable surface, or the two ends sit on parts of the level that do not connect. A refused call also stops an agent that was already walking somewhere. For a target that keeps moving, simply call it again — each call replans from where the agent stands. The point must lie on the NavMesh surface; the same x/z four metres above it is refused.

# On an entity with a Nav Agent. World positions on the baked NavMesh.
POINTS = [(6, 0, -6), (6, 0, 6), (-6, 0, 6)]

class Patrol(horizon.Behavior):
    def on_start(self):
        self.i = -1
        self.go_next()

    def go_next(self):
        self.i = (self.i + 1) % len(POINTS)
        if not horizon.nav.moveTo(self.entity_id, *POINTS[self.i]):
            horizon.log(f"patrol point {self.i} is not reachable")

        # isMoving turns false on arrival (and after a refusal).

rows.t:
Tells the character to move in a direction this frame; the length is the throttle, 0 to 1, and anything longer is cut back to 1. The direction is read as the Movement component's "Move Direction Is" says: World by default, the main camera's heading for a Player Character. Up and down are ignored. It has to be called every frame it should move — the intent is cleared at the end of each one, so a missed frame reads as "stopped" rather than as "keep going". Two calls in one frame add up. Does nothing, without a log line, on an entity without a Movement component. The Y component counts towards the length before it is dropped.

A Player Character gets both components automatically. The Movement system turns the request into velocity once per frame before physics steps. move is an intent for one frame: call it every frame the character should walk. The engine takes one snapshot per frame, so every query gives the same answer for the rest of that frame. Only a running game or play mode fills it; in the editor outside play the values are stale. For one-shot reactions prefer the action callbacks (onInputPressed and friends) over polling. Starts the emitter, or starts it again from the beginning. A one-shot that has already run needs this to run a second time: it resets the burst it has emitted, so firing the same effect twice fires it twice. Particles still in the air are left alone, which is what lets a fast repeat overlap its own tail.
Lua/Python

Stops the emitter producing anything more, while the particles already out live out their lifetime and fade normally. Deliberately not the same as hiding the entity, which leaves it simulating unseen, nor the same as a pause, which would freeze a cloud of smoke in mid-air.
Lua/Python

Emits a number of particles at once from an entity's Particle System, ignoring its emit rate entirely. This is what a hit, a muzzle flash or a footstep is: so many at a moment, which a rate cannot express — an emit rate high enough to look instant depends on the frame rate. It answers how many were actually made, which can be fewer than asked for when the emitter's Max Particles is already reached.
Lua/Python

Whether the effect is still running — either still emitting, or with particles still alive. It goes false the moment a one-shot has completely finished, which is how a graph waits for an effect instead of guessing a duration.
Lua/Python

Which widget draws over which: higher is nearer the front. For keeping a pause menu above a HUD. Takes the Widget from a Create Widget node.
Lua/Python

Is this widget on screen? A new widget starts visible, so this is false only after Hide Widget, or for a Widget that was destroyed.
Lua/Python

Calls a public function on the widget's own graph by name — the way the outside talks to a screen. Ok is false when the widget or the function is not there.
Lua/Python
addChild(widget: ref, parent: string, widgetAsset: string)

Puts another widget INSIDE this one, while it runs: the asset is grafted under the element you name, so a Vertical Box called "List" stacks a row per call. That is how a list of unknown length is built — a todo list, search results, a chat. The Child that comes back is a live object: Set External writes its public variables, Call External runs its functions, Bind Event listens to what it emits. 0 when the widget, the element or the asset is not there.
Lua/Python

Takes one of those rows out again, by the Child the Add gave you. Its elements and its logic both go. Ok is false when that child is not in this widget (already removed, or it belongs to another one).
Lua/Python

put in it, and says how many went. The short way to rebuild a list from scratch instead of tracking every row you added.
Lua/Python
setListCount(widget: ref, list: string, count: int)

Tells a ListView how many items there are. It keeps no items of its own: it works out which of them fit on screen, puts up only those rows, and asks you to fill each one in through On Row Bind. That is why ten thousand items cost ten rows instead of ten thousand elements. Name the list by the name its element has in the designer. Safe to call from inside On Row Bind — an endless list that loads more when its last row appears is written exactly that way; the new count takes effect on the next frame.
Lua/Python

How many items the list was last told it has. Not how many rows are on screen — that is the list's own business.
Lua/Python
listRow(widget: ref, list: string, index: int)

The live row showing that item, or 0 when it is scrolled out of sight. This is what an On Row Bind handler writes into: Set External for the row's public variables, Call External for its functions. Do not hold on to it — the same row is pointed at a different item as soon as the list scrolls.
Lua/Python

Asks every row on screen to be filled in again, without moving anything. What you call after sorting, filtering or editing your data: the list never saw it, so it cannot notice that it changed. The selection is by INDEX, so after a sort it points at whichever items now sit at those positions — remap it yourself if it has to follow the same rows. Calling this from inside On Row Bind is allowed: it takes effect on the next frame rather than looping back into the bind that asked for it.
Lua/Python
setListSelected(widget: ref, list: string, index: int, selected: bool)

Picks or unpicks one item. An index of -1 clears the selection. Does nothing when the list's Selection is None; in Single mode picking one drops the other. Fires On Selection Changed when the set really changed.
Lua/Python

The picked item's index, or -1 when nothing is picked. With Multiple selection this is the lowest of them.
Lua/Python
scrollListToItem(widget: ref, list: string, index: int)

Scrolls just far enough for that item to be fully visible, and does nothing when it already is — so stepping through a list does not re-centre it on every step.
Lua/Python
animate(widget: ref, element: string, property: string, to: float, seconds: float, easing: string)

Moves a NUMBER of one element from where it is to where you say, over the given seconds, along an easing curve ("Linear", "Out Quad", "Out Back"…). Opacity, corner radius, rotation, font size. Zero seconds writes it at once. Starting a second one on the same property replaces the first from wherever the value has got to, so a value can be retargeted mid-flight without a jump. OnAnimationFinished says when it lands, and names the property it was.
Lua/Python
animateColor(widget: ref, element: string, property: string, to: color, seconds: float, easing: string)

The same for a COLOUR — a fade, a flash, a hover that arrives instead of snapping. Every colour an element has can be animated, including a button's hovered and pressed ones.
Lua/Python
animateVec2(widget: ref, element: string, property: string, to: vec2, seconds: float, easing: string)

The same for a POINT: Position to slide something in, Size to grow it. "Out Back" is the curve that makes a dialog land rather than arrive.
Lua/Python
stopAnimation(widget: ref, element: string, property: string)

Stops what is running on that property, or on the whole element when the property is left empty. The value stays where it got to — a stop is not a rewind — and a stopped animation reports nothing, because cancelled is not finished.
Lua/Python
playAnimation(widget: ref, animation: string, restoreAfterCompleted: bool, direction: string)

Plays one of the animations the widget carries — the ones made in the Designer's timeline — picked from the dropdown. Leave Widget unwired and it plays this widget's own. Whether it loops is the animation's own decision. Direction runs it forwards, backwards, or out and back. Restore After Completed puts the properties it moved back the way they were when it finishes, which is the whole of "flash this and undo it". An embedded component's animations count too, so a page can play what its component brought with it. OnClipFinished says when it ends; a looping one never does, and never restores either.
Lua/Python
playAnimationLooped(widget: ref, animation: string, loop: bool, direction: string)

The same, but you decide about looping instead of the animation. For the case where one clip is both the spinner that runs until you stop it and the flourish that plays once.
Lua/Python

Stops that animation, or every one of the widget's when the name is left empty. Values stay where they got to, and nothing is reported — cancelled is not finished.
Lua/Python

Whether that animation is running right now. What a toggle asks before deciding which way to go.
Lua/Python

A reference to the component sitting in one of this widget's slots, by the slot's name. A component is a class like any other, so this is how you call its functions, bind its events and read its public variables — and how a page tells one of three identical cards apart. Leave Widget unwired for this widget's own slots.
Lua/Python

Stops everything moving in the widget: the authored animations and the single-property ones both. What a screen being torn down or swapped reaches for, because it does not have to name what it started. Values stay where they got to;

is the one that puts them back.
Lua/Python

Stops everything and puts every property an animation ever touched back the way it was BEFORE anything animated it — not the way it was a moment ago. Stopping is part of it: a clip left running would write over the restored values on the next frame. Outputs how many properties were put back, which is 0 when nothing had been animated.
Lua/Python

Puts this widget up as a DIALOG: the screen behind it dims, nothing under it can be clicked, scrolled or reached with the keyboard, and the focus starts inside it. It is raised above every other widget, so it cannot end up blocking input while drawing behind something. It stays until

, Escape or the Back button — that is what makes it modal.
Lua/Python
openPopup(widget: ref, x: float, y: float)

Puts the widget up at a point on screen — in render-target pixels — and lets a click anywhere else dismiss it. Its root elements are moved there and pushed back inside the screen, whatever anchors they were drawn with, so a menu near the bottom edge opens upwards instead of off the screen. No dimming: a popup is left by looking elsewhere, a dialog has to be answered.
Lua/Python

The same, at the mouse. This is the context menu: answer On Right Clicked with it and the menu appears where the click was. The engine remembers where the pointer last was, so the graph does not have to.
Lua/Python

Closes the topmost dialog, popup or open dropdown and says whether there was one. Exactly what Escape and the gamepad's Back button do — so a "Cancel" button is this node and nothing else. The widget that closes gets On Dismissed, and the keyboard focus goes back where it was before it opened. Hide Widget on a dialog does the same thing — hiding one IS closing it, so it lets go of the input, the focus and the dimming and fires On Dismissed too. This node is the one to reach for when you do not have the dialog's own id, which is the usual case for a Cancel button.

rows.t: run(exe: string, args: string[], timeoutSeconds: float)
ok: bool, exitCode: int, out: string, err: string

Runs another program and WAITS for it. Arguments go in one at a time — this is not a command line, so a path with a space in it needs no quoting and cannot inject anything. Four answers, because a caller who only wants to know whether it worked reads Ok, and one who has to explain a failure to a person needs the exit code and Err. A non-zero exit code is an ANSWER, not a breakage. It blocks the frame, so give it a timeout you are willing to wait; left at zero it is thirty seconds. Needs the project's "Run other programs" permission.
Lua/Python

Where the system would find this program, or empty if it would not find it at all. Deliberately needs NO permission: asking whether something is installed runs nothing, and it is how a script tells somebody what it would need before they decide to allow it.

Remember progress in the save game
Open a slot when play starts, read the level out of it, and write it back on F5.

vars.label: Lua
vars.text:
local M = {}

function M.onStart(self)
    if horizon.save.exists("slot1") then
        horizon.save.load("slot1")
    else
        horizon.save.create("slot1")
    end
    self.level   = horizon.save.getNumber("level", 1)  -- the default is required
    self.wasDown = false
end

function M.onUpdate(self, dt)
    local down = horizon.input.keyDown("F5")
    if down and not self.wasDown then      -- keyDown is a state, not an event
        horizon.save.setNumber("level", self.level)
        horizon.save.write()
    end
    self.wasDown = down
end

return M

A bone mask is a list of joint

with a weight each, not a skeleton: it works on every rig that spells its joints the same way. It is an allow-list — a joint that is not in it has weight 0 — and weights below 1 down a few spine joints are what fades a masked layer into the base pose instead of ending it at a hard edge across the waist.
component corrects the finished pose against the world the character is standing in. Two independent halves:

puts each foot on the ground actually under it — a ray down from the foot, a two-bone solve up the leg, the foot tilted to the surface normal within a pitch and roll limit, and the pelvis lowered by the deepest foot's drop so the low leg does not have to overextend — and
turns a chain of joints (spine, neck, head) towards a target entity or a world point, within a yaw and pitch limit, with the turn spread over the chain by weight.

Both are smoothed over time, because the ground under a foot really does jump by a whole step height in one frame at a stair edge; a character that is teleported is detected as such and snaps instead of easing. Foot placement needs a physics world, so it runs in play mode only and does nothing where there is no collider; look-at runs in the editor too.
The order a pose is built in

Each stage holds whatever the one before it came up with, and the order is fixed: the animator (clip, blend or state machine) decides the pose, root motion is taken out of it and turned into entity movement, the layer stack is applied on top of what is left, and inverse kinematics bends the result to the world. That order is what makes the four safe to add one at a time — and it is why an additive layer that moves the root joint moves the pose rather than the character.

bone overlay, and an optional clip slot with play/pause and time scrubbing — inspect a rig without touching any scene.

sections.text: Input is asset-driven: instead of hard-coding key codes, you declare logical Input Actions and bind them in an Input Mapping Context. Input Action — a named action with a value type: Button (pressed/released) or Axis (−1…1). The asset name is the action name (e.g. IA_Jump). Input Mapping Context — binds keys and gamepad buttons to actions, and key pairs, button pairs, mouse sources or gamepad sticks/triggers (with scales) to axes. In HorizonCode projects, Player Controller and Player Character classes are spawned automatically when play begins; each mapped action arrives as graph events — Input.<Action>.Pressed, Input.<Action>.Released and Input.<Action>.Axis — alongside BeginPlay and a per-frame Tick. Gamepads work through the same assets: bind a pad button next to the keys, or pick a stick/trigger as an axis source, and the same Input.<Action>.* events fire — no script changes. All connected controllers merge into one virtual pad (single player), sticks get a radial deadzone (tunable in the editor settings), and the camera rig has its own stick sensitivity in degrees per second, separate from the mouse's per-pixel value. Button and axis names are SDL's mapping strings in Xbox-layout positions: a is the south button (Cross on a PlayStation pad), leftshoulder, dpup; axes are leftx, righty, lefttrigger, … Stick Y is positive downward — bind with scale −1 for an up-positive axis. Scripts can also poll input directly: input.keyDown("Space"), input.mouseButton, input.mousePosition, input.mouseDelta, input.scrollDelta — and the pad: input.gamepadConnected(), input.gamepadButton("a"), input.gamepadAxis("leftx") (deadzone-filtered; a resting stick reads exactly 0). While the game is paused: a pause (time.setTimeScale(0)) silences every action by default — otherwise the player keeps shooting through the pause menu. Each Input Action has a Fires while the game is paused switch for the few that must get through anyway: opening and closing the menu, navigating it, confirming. Presses that arrive while a silenced action is paused are dropped, not queued for the moment the game resumes; a key held across the pause is not mistaken for a fresh press either. Direct polling (input.keyDown and friends) is never gated.

sections.text: The Widget Designer: element palette, canvas and per-element details The Designer is a UMG-style layout editor: Palette — the nine element types; click or drag onto the canvas. Dropping onto a Panel nests the new element inside it. Hierarchy — the element tree; children move with their parents. Canvas — WYSIWYG editing with drag-to-move, resize handles, zoom and pan. Details — every property of the selected element, plus an Events section: clicking an event (e.g. + OnClicked) jumps to Graph mode and spawns the matching event node. Layout: anchors & pivots Every element has a position, size, pivot and a 9-point anchor (top-left … bottom-right). The anchor picks the reference corner inside the parent (root elements anchor to the canvas), the position offsets from it and the pivot shifts the element's own origin — so UIs scale cleanly to any resolution. A layer value orders siblings; visibility cascades down the tree. Elements can also carry a node-graph material (animated backgrounds, procedural effects — parameters settable at runtime) and a custom font asset, and define their pointer behaviour: hit-testable or click-through, plus a hover cursor (arrow, hand, text, resize …).

local M = {}

function M.onStart(self)
    -- spawn the HUD widget and keep its id
    self.hud = horizon.createWidget("UI/HUD")
    horizon.setWidgetZOrder(self.hud, 10)
end

function M.onUpdate(self, dt)
    if horizon.isWidgetVisible(self.hud) then
        horizon.callWidgetFunction(self.hud, "Refresh")
    end
end

return M

sections.text: For UI that belongs to the scene — a name tag over a character, a world-space info panel — entities can carry the canvas-based UI components: UI Canvas (screen-space or world-space, virtual resolution), UI Element (anchored rect with pivot, rotation and layer), UI Text, UI Image (material + tint) and UI Button (state colours + an on-click script function). Scripts address these through the entity UI calls — setUIText, setUIColor, setUIVisible, setUIPosition, setUISize, setUIMaterialParam — and scripts on the entity receive onClick, onHoverEnter and onHoverExit. Which one to use? Menus, HUDs and anything that should survive scene changes -> UI Widgets. Labels and panels attached to things in the world -> entity UI.
